open_questions: A Night in Tunisia (1960): the only human Songsterr tab (4268119) is in six-bar blocks that do not follow the tune's form, so it was not used; find a transcription.
Blues March's head and solos and the solos of Afrique, The Egyptian, The Core and It Ain't Necessarily So are reconstructions: Bishop transcribes the intros, grooves and the Afrique solo only.
The Drum Thunder Suite (Songsterr 5198319, 'retranscribed') reads like a rock groove in places; check it against the record before using it.
The press roll is named everywhere (Taylor 1977, Bishop) but no bar of it was transcribed: write one from a record.
His kit by year: the 1958 film shows a Gretsch in a light sparkle; Ludwig and other makes later are not sourced here.
John Ramsey's Art Blakey's Jazz Messages (1994) and Chip Stern's 1984 Modern Drummer style analysis were not read.

identity.name: Art Blakey
home_scenes: Billy Eckstine's big band and 52nd Street bebop (1940s)

alter_egos.name: Abdullah Ibn Buhaina
alter_egos.context: The Muslim name he took in the late 1940s; 'Bu' to his musicians.

identity.summary: With Kenny Clarke and Max Roach, one of the makers of modern jazz drumming, and for thirty-five years the leader of the Jazz Messengers, the school of hard bop through which Lee Morgan, Wayne Shorter, Freddie Hubbard and Wynton Marsalis passed. The ride with the hi-hat foot slammed shut on 2 and 4, the snare's backbeat in the 'original jazz shuffle' of Moanin', a press roll to bring in each soloist, and Afro and Latin grooves on the cymbal's bell and the toms: Blues March's drum cadence, Afrique's vamp in three, El Toro's bell, The Core's threes over four. He played loud, and long: 'that simple, sustained, deep, powerful, groove' (Todd Bishop).

traditions.impact: Chick Webb, Sid Catlett and Ray Bauduc in his early style; 'So many people helped me to come up in this field—Sid Catlett, Gene Krupa, Chick Webb, Max Roach, Kenny Clarke'. Webb had him roll ''til you get to one hundred'; Catlett told him to 'just roll'.

A trip in the late 1940s, 'just to learn ... to find out what was happening', where he accepted Islam; 'all my life I've been trying to bring that together with the African rhythms.' Rapping the drum's side and pressing the tom with his elbow to bend its pitch.

formative_events.event: Self-taught: piano at school, playing for money by seventh grade, then drums in the early 1930s.
Billy Eckstine's big band, to 1947, with the bebop players.
A Night at Birdland with Clifford Brown and Horace Silver; the Jazz Messengers with Silver, his own band from 1956.

eras.label: Eckstine, Monk and bebop
eras.context: Billy Eckstine's band, then Monk, Parker, Gillespie and Bud Powell; Buddy DeFranco's quartet (1951-53).

eras.label: The classic Jazz Messengers
eras.context: Blue Note records at Van Gelder's: Moanin' (1958) with Lee Morgan and Benny Golson, then Wayne Shorter's band and the sextet with Freddie Hubbard and Curtis Fuller; sideman dates with Milt Jackson and Grant Green.

eras.label: The later Messengers
eras.context: The band as a school: Woody Shaw, Bobby Watson, the Marsalis brothers, Terence Blanchard; Ralph Peterson Jr. as a second drummer from 1983.

evidence.note: 'The attack of the ride cymbal is a little ahead of the bass, and the snare drum is behind everything— playing the shuffle rhythm the way he does is a way of getting that behind-the-beat feel.'

swing.notes: Swung eighths at medium and up tempos; the shuffle's pick-up 'is not a triplet' on Plenty, Plenty Soul; the Afro 6 and Latin heads straight or in triplets.

dynamics.balance: Uniformly loud in the Afrique solo, 'basically every note is accented'; a dramatic change of level with each new soloist (Bishop).

feel_profile.interaction: No bebop-type comping on Plenty, Plenty Soul: 'he makes big statements here and there; usually at the end of a solo, leading into the next solo'; the press roll or tom triplets between soloists (Bishop).

hand_techniques.name: The press roll
hand_techniques.description: A crescendoing multiple-bounce roll into the next soloist's chorus, played 'technically wrong, but it's the way I feel'.

hand_techniques.name: Pitch bends
hand_techniques.description: The snares off, one stick or an elbow pressed into the head to bend a tom or the snare (Afrique's solo, Safari, Plenty, Plenty Soul).

hand_techniques.name: Flat flams and multiple-bounce rolls
hand_techniques.description: Blues March's cadence: 5-, 9- and 13-stroke multiple-bounce rolls, flams played 'pretty flat'.

foot_techniques.name: The hat foot on 2 and 4
foot_techniques.description: 'The forceful closing of the hi-hat on every second and fourth beat.'

foot_techniques.name: Feathered quarters
foot_techniques.description: The bass drum 'patted' in quarters, heard on accents and with the band's kicks.

coordination.notes: Max Roach: 'perhaps the best at maintaining independence with all four limbs' (Wikipedia).

devices.description: The Core: snare and hat foot every three eighths, the cymbal and the kick an eighth after each, so the bar runs in threes across the 4/4 'off of this piano figure'; in parts of the solos 'he'll extend playing in 3 over 4/4 time a la Elvin'.

evidence.note: Bishop's two two-bar examples; 'it gets pretty raggedy, so the transcription hardly does it justice'.

devices.description: The Egyptian's intro: flammed buzz rolls in quarter-note triplets, three across each half of the bar, and in bar 20 buzzes 'LH only' with the toms.

evidence.note: Bishop's transcription, bars 4, 20 and 22.

devices.description: Afrique: the vamp in three, and into the solos 'a metric modulation into 4/4— the dotted quarter during this intro groove becomes the quarter note'.

evidence.note: Bishop: the vamp at quarter = 214 in 3/4, the solo at 140.

devices.description: El Toro and Johnny's Blue: a bell pattern with 'that little syncopated move across the barline that we see a few years later in the Mozambique rhythm'.

searched: Todd Bishop's Blakey transcriptions and grooves on cruiseshipdrummer.com, read from their images and PDFs: Blues March (2017), Afrique groove and solo (2017), It Ain't Necessarily So's Afro (2014), Johnny's Blue and El Toro (2020), the Japan tom-tom groove (2020), Plenty, Plenty Soul (2020), The Egyptian intro (2019), The Core (2022)
Songsterr human drum tabs: Moanin' 909920; A Night in Tunisia 4268119 and The Drum Thunder Suite 5198319 read and not used
Wikipedia: Art Blakey; Les Tomkins's interviews (1963, 1973, 1987); Arthur Taylor's Notes and Tones (via Scott K Fish)
devices_search.note: Four devices, each from a transcription. The triplets of his solos (Afrique) are a subdivision, not a cross pulse; Ken Burns's notes of 'accents in triplets or cross-rhythms' name no record, so no device rests on them alone. A Night in Tunisia's tom-tom groove is a lead Bishop did not confirm on the record.

voice_language.snare: The backbeat on 2 and 4 in the shuffles; flams and multiple-bounce rolls in the march; the press roll; rim clicks in the Afro and Latin grooves.
voice_language.kick: Feathered quarters, or the kick with the band's figures; in the Afrique solo on every triplet.
voice_language.toms: Afro and Latin grooves on the toms, pitch bends, triplets round the toms at the end of a solo.
voice_language.hihat: The foot slammed shut on 2 and 4, on every 'and' in the double time.
voice_language.cymbals: One heavy 20-inch K. Zildjian ride, a dark, complex sound ridden hard; the bell for the Latin and Afro grooves.

aesthetic: Rudy Van Gelder's Blue Note room
sound_profile.cymbal_character: A heavy 20-inch K. Zildjian ride on The Big Beat and Indestructible; 'one 20″ sizzle cymbal' on Plenty, Plenty Soul (Bishop).

by_era.description: A Gretsch in a light sparkle (the 1958 film), one tom and a floor tom; the snares off for the pitch-bend passages.

sample_hints.50s: A small jazz kit, a dark heavy ride, the hat foot loud.

signature_traits.label: The press roll
signature_traits.description: A crescendoing press roll, 'a Blakey trademark', that brings in the next soloist.

signature_traits.label: The hat slammed on 2 and 4
signature_traits.description: The hi-hat foot closed hard on every second and fourth beat, under everything.

signature_traits.label: The jazz shuffle
signature_traits.description: A backbeat on the snare with a pick-up before it under the ride: Moanin', 'the original jazz shuffle', and Plenty, Plenty Soul.

signature_traits.label: Afro and Latin heads
signature_traits.description: Grooves of his own on the bell and toms for the head, the solos swung: Afrique, It Ain't Necessarily So, El Toro, Avila and Tequila.

signature_traits.label: Loud and sustained
signature_traits.description: 'He played with such force and fury that he eventually lost much of his hearing'; 'simple, sustained, deep, powerful, groove'.

patterns.name: Moanin': the time under the solos
patterns.function: The ride's skip beat, the kick on 1 and 3, the snare and the hat foot on 2 and 4: the jazz shuffle.

evidence.note: The tab's commonest bar (203 of 308), straight eighths to be swung; the tab writes no hat foot, added from his trademark (Wikipedia).

patterns.name: Moanin': the call and the Amen
patterns.function: The piano's call bar left to the hat foot, then the band's Amen on the ride, on 3 and the 'and' of 4.

evidence.note: Head bars 1-2 (and 3-16, 25-32); hat foot added.

patterns.name: Blues March: the drum intro
patterns.function: Snare eighths swung, flams on the 'and' of 1 and on 2 and 4, short multiple-bounce rolls on the 'and's of 2 and 4; then triplets on 1 and 2.

evidence.note: Bishop's bars 1-2 on a grid of six to the beat; a flam with a roll on it is written as the roll.

patterns.name: Blues March: the cadence
patterns.function: Accents on 1 and 2, a half-note roll on 3, the kick and the hat foot on every beat.

evidence.note: Bishop's bars 5-7.

patterns.name: Blues March: the roll-off
patterns.function: Straight eighths: snare and kick on 1 and its 'and', a roll into 3, snare and kick on 3 and its 'and', the snare on the 'and' of 4; then a roll, and the cymbal on 3, its 'and' and 4.

evidence.note: Bishop's bars 9-10.

patterns.name: Plenty, Plenty Soul: the shuffle backbeat
patterns.function: The cymbal's dotted-eighth and sixteenth, the backbeat on 2 and 4 with the shuffle pick-up before it, the bass drum feathered.

evidence.note: Written from Bishop's description; 'it's not a triplet'. The hat foot on 2 and 4 is assumed.

patterns.name: Plenty, Plenty Soul: the double time
patterns.function: The cymbal's dotted rhythm and the backbeat, the hat foot on every 'and'.

evidence.note: Bishop's notated bar.

patterns.name: Afrique: the vamp in three
patterns.function: The ride in eighths, the kick on 1, the hat foot on the 'and' of 2, the low tom on 3; then the ride on 1, 2, 3 and its 'and', the high tom on the 'and' of 2 and on 3.

evidence.note: Bishop's groove o' the day, written in 3/4.

patterns.name: Afrique: the solo's triplets
patterns.function: The bass drum on every triplet, two on the snare and one on the high tom to each beat, every note accented.

evidence.note: Bars 10-13 of Bishop's transcription.

patterns.name: It Ain't Necessarily So: the Afro 6
patterns.function: The cymbal's bell on every eighth but the second, a rim click on 1 and on the second eighth of 2, the high tom, the floor tom softly on 4, the kick barely on 1 and 3, the foot on 2 and 4.

evidence.note: Bishop's groove o' the day; the tempo is the dotted quarter.

patterns.name: El Toro: the Latin groove
patterns.function: The bell on 1, 2, 3, 4 and their 'and's but 2's, then across the bar line on the 'and' of 1; the low tom on 2 and its 'and', the high tom on 4 and its 'and'; no audible bass drum.

evidence.note: Bishop's two bars.

patterns.name: The Egyptian: the intro's figure
patterns.function: The ride on 1, 2, the 'and' of 2 with the kick, 3, 4 and its 'and', the kick on 1, the hat foot on 4.

evidence.note: Bishop bars 3, 17, 21.

patterns.name: The Egyptian: snare triplets
patterns.function: The ride on each beat, the snare on the two triplets after it, the second accented.

evidence.note: Bishop bars 2, 10, 12.

patterns.name: The Egyptian: quarter-note triplets of rolls
patterns.function: Flammed buzz rolls in quarter-note triplets over the bar, the hat foot on 2 and 4.

evidence.note: Bishop bars 4 and 22.

patterns.name: The Core: the rubadub
patterns.function: Snare and hat foot every three eighths, the cymbal and the kick an eighth after each, running over the bar line; the second bar answers.

evidence.note: Bishop's first two-bar example; the second bar's triplet is written as two eighths.

equipment.label: Gretsch, late 1950s
equipment.layout_notes: The 1958 film: a Gretsch in a light sparkle, the band's name on the bass drum's head, one tom on the bass drum and a floor tom, chrome stands. The K ride from Bishop (The Egyptian, The Big Beat). The end year is a guess.

affiliations.name: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers
affiliations.notes: Co-led with Horace Silver at first; his own from 1956.

affiliations.name: Thelonious Monk
affiliations.notes: 'Thelonious Monk was the guy that was keeping me busy, recording and things.'

evidence.note: An early influence; Webb had him roll ''til you get to one hundred'.
'Just roll.'
He thanks 'Horace, Kenny and the guys' for the Messengers' start; with Clarke and Roach, the makers of modern drumming.
Each names the other: Blakey among those who 'helped me to come up', Roach that he was 'perhaps the best at maintaining independence with all four limbs'.
Joined in 1983 as a second drummer.
'Art kept it going.'

philosophy.idea: Nobody should tell you how to do it: play the roll the way you feel it, whichever end of the stick.
The one is always there; you need not keep counting it, so explore over it.
The band is a school: young players come in, develop and go out on their own.

innovations: Hard bop drumming: the shuffle backbeat, the press roll and the hat on 2 and 4 driving a small band
Afro and Latin grooves of his own as jazz heads
The Jazz Messengers as a school for young musicians

cultural_references.description: Ralph Peterson Jr.: 'every bit as polyrhythmic as Elvin Jones' (Wikipedia).

common_misconceptions: That his playing was only loud: on Plenty, Plenty Soul it is 'clean, understated', 'like a hired studio drummer' (Bishop).

beatbreaker.default_kit_sound: A small 1950s jazz kit, a heavy dark ride, the hat foot loud
generation_rules: The hat foot on 2 and 4, always.
A press roll into the next chorus at the end of a solo.
A backbeat on the snare in the shuffles, with its pick-up.
The head of an Afro or Latin tune on the bell and toms, the solos swung.
avoid: Busy bebop comping on the snare

lineage_display.lineage_blurb: Chick Webb's and Sid Catlett's rolls, Kenny Clarke's bebop and a trip to West Africa; and after him Tony Williams, Cindy Blackman, Tony Allen and a band's worth of Messengers.
